alalal-c42642-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 1: whether God is everywhere and in every thing.

alalal-c42642-d1e111.summary: Before treating the text, Albert lists four questions: whether God is everywhere and in every thing; whether being everywhere is the same as being in every thing; whether being everywhere is the same as being in every place and being wherever; and whether being everywhere belongs to God from eternity. This article treats the first.

alalal-c42642-d1e133.summary: First argument for omnipresence: taking the world as the whole of creation, the world is conserved in being everywhere; what conserves stands to the conserved as cause, distinct from it, so the conserver is neither the world nor part of it; such a conserver present everywhere can only be God.
claims: The conserver of the whole universe must be distinct from it and present wherever it is conserved, and this is God.

alalal-c42642-d1e173.summary: Rebuts the reply that God conserves through an infused power distinct from himself, as a generator gives dispositions that resist corruption. Giving being and conserving belong to the same agent, and the infused power itself needs conserving, not by itself, so by another; if that is created there is an infinite regress, so the conserver must be God, who is thus everywhere.
claims: Conservation cannot be delegated to a created power without infinite regress.

alalal-c42642-d1e223.summary: Argues from Anselm's definition of God as that than which nothing greater can be thought: if God were only inside or only outside things he would be bounded, and something greater could be thought. He must be inside, outside, above and beneath all things, hence everywhere.
claims: A God confined inside or outside things would be bounded and so not maximal.

alalal-c42642-d1e252.summary: Argues from Gregory that what was made from nothing would tend back to nothing unless held by the Almighty's hand. Since things were made from nothing everywhere, the one who holds them must be everywhere.
claims: Creatures made from nothing require a sustaining presence everywhere.

alalal-c42642-d1e270.summary: Argues from John Damascene that God falls short of perfection in no respect, including place; to fall short in place is not to be everywhere, so God is everywhere.
claims: Omnipresence follows from God's perfection in every respect.

alalal-c42642-d1e299.summary: Argues that the power to conserve oneself in being implies no need and so belongs to God alone. Since every creature depends on what it comes from, this power cannot be given to any place or part of the world, so God conserves the world immediately and is everywhere.
claims: Self-conservation belongs only to God, so creatures are conserved immediately by him.

alalal-c42642-d1e321.summary: Even granting that God gave the world a power to conserve itself, that habitual power must be received from God, and between receiver and giver there is essential contact unless a medium carries the influence. No medium can stand between one who draws a thing out of nothing and what is drawn out, so God must be present everywhere.
claims: No medium can intervene between the creator and what is drawn from nothing.

alalal-c42642-d1e357.summary: Argues from exemplarity: every creature has an exemplar in God, and what is noble in creatures is attributed to God. In place and the located, distinction belongs to ignobility, arising from diversity and divisibility of matter, while containing, filling and preserving are noble. Removing distinction and attributing the rest to God yields that God fills, contains and preserves every place and thing.
claims: The noble features of place, filling, containing and preserving, belong eminently to God without spatial distinction.

alalal-c42642-d1e409.summary: Argues from the universal. Universality may be by species, genus or analogy, the last being most universal. Being in many belongs to ignobility, since the universal is contracted and perishes with its particulars; being said of many belongs to nobility, giving it extension everywhere and always. Since the analogical universal is exemplified from divine being and is in every thing, God must be even more so, since the exemplified falls short of the exemplar.
claims: If even the analogical universal is everywhere, God, its exemplar, is all the more so.
concepts: esse in multis vs de multis

alalal-c42642-d1e490.summary: Argues from the order of causes: the first cause in a natural order remains in all secondary ones essentially, presentially and potentially, though contracted, which is ignoble; hence some philosophers called unity the first form constituting all others. Removing the ignobility, the first of all causes is in all things in these three ways. Being, living and sensing, and the successive grades of matter, illustrate how prior formal causes remain in posterior ones.
claims: The first cause is present in all secondary causes essentially, presentially and potentially.

alalal-c42642-d1e553.summary: Concludes the proofs, noting that certain so-called philosophers deny that God is everywhere, and introduces their counterarguments.

alalal-c42642-d1e566.summary: First philosophical objection: it is nobler to make works that remain without the maker than works that remain only in his presence, and God's works are perfect (Deuteronomy 32), so they remain even when he is separated from them.

alalal-c42642-d1e584.summary: Second objection: a lower craftsman, like a carpenter, can make lasting works without remaining present, so much more can the highest craftsman.

alalal-c42642-d1e594.summary: Third objection: nature does this, since a generator gives both the species and the dispositions that conserve it against corrupting alterations; so God does likewise.

alalal-c42642-d1e610.summary: Fourth objection: a king who can govern only when present is weak, so it would be a sign of weakness in God if he could hold creatures only by being present.

alalal-c42642-d1e623.summary: Fifth, stronger objection: the most efficacious heavenly powers act and conserve not immediately but through the elements; since God is more like what is noble, he too would act through intermediaries.

alalal-c42642-d1e639.summary: Sixth objection: if God is everywhere by essence, presence and power, he does everything, so no nature has its own operation, contrary to Damascene and all the philosophical sciences.

alalal-c42642-d1e663.summary: Seventh objection: the argument from the order of causes holds only for essential, i.e. formal, causes. Among efficient causes the first is in the second only by power, not by essence or presence, and God is an efficient cause of things, not their form or matter.

alalal-c42642-d1e689.summary: Solution: the initial arguments conclude the truth that God is everywhere.
claims: God is everywhere.

alalal-c42642-d1e697.summary: Reply to the first objection: it is simply false that it is nobler to make works that last without the maker. Whatever conserves a thing comes from some cause prior to it, efficient, formal or material; in God's making nothing precedes the work but God, so it can be conserved only by him, essentially present.
claims: Since nothing pre-exists God's work but God, the work can be conserved only by God's essential presence.

alalal-c42642-d1e735.summary: Explains why lower craftsmen's works last without them: some pre-existing matter conserves the impressed form, as wax holds a seal's form while water does not. Nature too works on pre-existing matter, though differently from art, since nature makes form out of matter while art works in matter. This answers the three following objections.
claims: Created agents' works outlast them only because pre-existing matter retains the form; God's creation has no such substrate.

alalal-c42642-d1e790.summary: Reply on the heavenly powers: they move diverse things by their diverse positions and so must be distant from generable matter, but all this, apart from moving itself, is imperfection; what achieves goodness by one motion is better than what needs many, so God need not resemble them in this.
claims: Mediated celestial causation reflects imperfection and should not be attributed to God.

alalal-c42642-d1e829.summary: Reply on proper operations: the objection holds only if there were one cause. The first cause is immediately present to all precisely so that they can have their own operations and causes; the two are not in the same genus of causality, since God does not mix with things and so does not take away their nature. On the king: in spatial agents, power extending beyond essence shows a more limited essence, but in God essence is commensurate with power, neither limited by place.
claims: God's immediate presence grounds rather than displaces the proper causality of creatures.
In God, essence is as unlimited as power, so he acts where he is.

alalal-c42642-d1e881.summary: Reply on efficient causes: in nature efficient causes are ordered and touch one another only through influence, since their essence is less than their power; this is imperfection and is not attributed to God.
claims: Action at a distance through influence is an imperfection not found in God.

alalal-c42642.summary: Article 1 asks whether God is everywhere and in every thing, after listing the four questions the distinction raises. Nine arguments prove that he is: from the conservation of the universe, which cannot be delegated to a created power without regress; from Anselm's maximal being; from Gregory on creatures' tendency to nothing; from Damascene on divine perfection; from self-conservation as God's alone; from the absence of any medium between creator and creature; from exemplarism and the analogical universal; and from the presence of the first cause in all secondary causes. Seven philosophical objections hold that works can last without their maker and that God, like the heavens or a king, acts through intermediaries or would leave natures no operation of their own. Albert replies that God's works can be conserved only by him, since nothing pre-exists them, while created craftsmen rely on matter that retains form. Mediation and power exceeding essence are imperfections, and God's immediate presence grounds rather than suppresses the proper operations of creatures, since he is not in the same genus of cause.
claims: God is everywhere and in every thing, conserving creation immediately.
Conservation of creatures cannot be delegated to any created power.
God's immediate causality does not compete with, but grounds, the proper causality of creatures.
Action through intermediaries and power exceeding essence are imperfections not attributable to God.
